name: British modernist studio ceramics
summary: Fine studio ceramics from London after 1946. Lucie Rie and Hans Coper worked in a small studio and made thin bowls, bottles and sculptural forms with a quiet, textured surface.

philosophy.core_thesis: A modern pot is a precise form with a quiet surface, where the glaze and the clay do the work that ornament did before.
design_principles: Throw the form thin and exact: a porcelain wall of 2 to 3 mm and a stoneware wall of 3 to 6 mm.
Keep the profile simple: a cylinder, a cone, a sphere or a combination of them.
Join two or three thrown parts with a visible rim, to make a form that is not a single throw.
Coat the stoneware with a thin manganese or a white slip, and leave it matt and unglazed.
Make the glaze pitted, volcanic or thick, in one colour, such as pink, yellow, white or bronze.
Scratch a line through a slip or a glaze with a pointed tool, in a pattern of 1 to 2 mm lines.
Fire in an electric kiln, in oxidation, at 1200 to 1280 °C.
Make a small number of pieces and a small range of forms.
anti_patterns: Pieces that repeat a mould with no variation
A form that is large and loud

form.shape: Bottles, shallow and deep bowls, cylinder vases, spade and cup forms, and sculptural vessels with a flat disc or a stem.
form.profile: A clear geometric profile: a sphere on a stem, a cone with a flat rim, a wide bowl with a thin, steep wall.
form.foot_and_rim: A very small foot, or a bare disc base; the rim is sharp and thin, or a flat disc that is an essential part of the form.
form.proportion: Height 8 to 35 cm; porcelain wall 2 to 3 mm and stoneware wall 3 to 6 mm; the foot is one third of the width or less.
rules: Make the profile exact, and check it with a template.
Join two or more thrown parts for a non-round or a stacked form.
Keep the colour to one tone and the surface to one texture.

bodies.rule: Use a fine white or dark stoneware and a hard porcelain. Do not use an earthenware, which cannot give the thin hard wall.

methods: turning and trimming of the foot
forming.joins: Two or three thrown parts are luted with slip and finished in the leather-hard state, to make a clear, firm seam.
forming.details: A thin rim, a bare disc foot, a pitted or textured glaze, a line scratched in the slip and a small impressed seal.

glaze.pattern: A single glaze that is pitted, volcanic or thick; a band of fine scratched lines; a matt manganese coat with a pale rim.
glaze.gloss: Matt to satin, 5 to 40 GU; the surface is quiet and not shiny.
glaze.wear: The matt surface marks easily, and the unglazed band shows the finger marks; the porcelain is hard and keeps its edge.

palette.strategy: A very limited palette of one quiet tone for each piece: white, pink, yellow, bronze or black.

firing.kiln: An electric kiln, with an even oxidation.
processes: a second firing for a thick or pitted glaze
firing.scale: One small studio of two to four workers, with a few hundred pieces a year.
firing.signs: A pitted glaze, a faint seam at the join, a scratched line and a pale unglazed band.

emotion.target_response: A feeling of quiet and balance: the viewer sees a precise, soft-coloured form and slows down.

use_cases: a refined bowl or bottle for a modern interior
a museum label on British modernist ceramics
avoid_when: the brief needs rustic, wood-fired pottery

modifiers.how: Use a thicker stoneware wall, an ash or tenmoku glaze and a wood-fired surface.
Break the profile, tear the thrown form and fire it with a thick, rough glaze.

wall_thickness.note: Rie porcelain walls are 2 to 3 mm thick; Coper stoneware is thicker.
